sections.hypothesis: Weeks that start after US dollar net liquidity has grown over 4 weeks are followed by better BTC (ETH) returns than weeks after it shrank.
sections.rationale: Who pays: crypto is a marginal, leveraged risk asset; when the Fed's balance sheet adds reserves, and the Treasury's cash account and the reverse repo facility don't soak them up, more dollars chase risk, and when they drain, the marginal buyer leaves. 'Net liquidity' (Fed assets minus the Treasury General Account minus reverse repo) is a widely followed practitioner gauge; the academic evidence is mixed (checked 2026-11-22): the New York Fed (Staff Report 1052, 2023) finds Bitcoin doesn't respond to surprise rate changes, and the IMF (WP/23/163, 'The Crypto Cycle and US Monetary Policy') finds Fed policy drives crypto's co-movement with equities, mostly through the policy rate rather than the balance sheet. This exact measure is practitioner commentary; the outside evidence is weak and the note says so. Weak point, stated now: 2018-25 holds only two or three liquidity cycles, so few independent episodes, and weekly weeks next to each other share the same cycle. Not a rejected family.
sections.rules: kestrel signal-study net-liquidity BTCUSDT ETHUSDT. Net liquidity each Wednesday = WALCL (Fed total assets) - WTREGEN (Treasury General Account) - RRPONTSYD (overnight reverse repo), from FRED, in the same units. Wednesday's H.4.1 figures are published Thursday afternoon US time, so a Wednesday value counts from the following Saturday 00:00 UTC (conservative). The signal at a Sunday close is on when the latest known Wednesday value is above the value 4 weeks before it. Span: 2018-01 to 2025-10. Each Sunday's daily close (UTC) is a sample; outcome: the log return of the Binance coin to the next Sunday's close. Samples a week apart never overlap; BTC and ETH are pooled (they move together, so the effective sample is smaller than the count). Never the holdout. Run once.
sections.falsification: PROCEED only if P(spread > 0) is at least 90% (bootstrap), the spread (mean week after 'on' minus mean week after 'off') beats one round trip of costs (about 22 bps), and the independence control holds. Otherwise KILL. A PROCEED leads to a strategy note on the full scorecard (BTC and ETH's holdout years are spent, so it would be judged forward on paper); a KILL ends it. Its overlap with the pursued strategies is reported beside the result, deciding nothing. The independence control, fixed here: the spread is also measured separately in weeks whose past week rose and weeks whose past week fell. PROCEED needs the spread positive in both halves as well; if it lives in only one, the signal is momentum (or dip-buying, a rejected family) under another name, and that is a KILL, said plainly.
sections.parameters: None to choose: 4 weeks (as the stablecoin study) and the Saturday rule fixed here.
sections.costs: A study: one look. Data: FRED's public CSVs (free, no key). FRED serves today's revised figures, not what was published at the time; H.4.1 revisions are rare and small, a caveat.

history.reason: Rejected (Luke, 2026-11-22). KILL (findings 22): spread -0.71%, P 17%, negative after rising and falling weeks alike.
